topic.title: IT services raise budgets
topic.claim: In IT services, the raise budget is fixed before ratings; the sector sets the cake, the rating cuts the slice.
topic.moment: Appraisal letter day: 'meets expectations plus' and a single-digit hike.

turn.actually: the company fixes a raise budget first; ratings only split it, and IT services has the smallest budget of any sector

topic.because: companies set merit budgets from margins and market benchmarks; services runs on thinner margins, so its pool is smaller
topic.payoff: Your rating decides your slice. Your sector decides the cake.

proof.fact: Aon projects India's average salary increase at 9.1% for 2027; Technology Consulting and Services 6.6% in both 2026 and 2027, the lowest of any sector; Technology Platform and Products 9.5%; NBFCs 10.1%
TCS 2026 hikes: top bands about 10-13%, lowest bands about 2-3%

paragraphs: In IT services, your raise budget was fixed before your manager rated you. The rating only decides how it gets split.
slides.why_swipe: it overturns what every salaried reader believes about appraisals

paragraphs: Letter day. "Meets expectations plus." Nice. You scroll down. Single digit.
Then the replay starts: every sprint, every 1:1, looking for what you did wrong.
slides.why_swipe: the reader has lived this; what actually decided it?

paragraphs: First, the company fixes a raise budget, guided by its margins and what the market is paying. Then the ratings happen.
The split is steep. At TCS this year, employees reported 9-13% in the top band, and little or no change in the lowest.
slides.why_swipe: if the budget is fixed first, how big is yours?

paragraphs: Aon's 2027 projections. India's average raise: 9.1%. Tech products: 9.5%. NBFCs: 10.1%.
IT services: 6.6%, the lowest of any sector, and the same as this year.
slides.why_swipe: 'the lowest of any sector' stings; what does it mean for the next ten years?

big.label: IT services vs tech products, 2027 raise budgets

paragraphs: So yes, your rating matters. It moves you around inside the budget.
But the budget comes from the business you're in. A top rating in services is still fighting over a smaller cake than the product company down the road.
slides.why_swipe: the concession makes the turn credible; the payoff is next

paragraphs: Move to products and, if this gap holds, every raise comes out of a bigger budget. That compounds.
**Your rating decides your slice. Your sector decides the cake.**

mechanism.actual_mechanism: Salary-increase (merit) budgets are set top-down months before appraisals: Finance and HR size a pool as a percentage of payroll using revenue/margin forecasts, inflation and external market benchmarks like Aon's survey, which is precisely what the 6.6% IT-services vs 9.5% tech-products figures measure — budgets, not outcomes. Managers then distribute that fixed pool through a merit matrix keyed to performance ratings, so a rating redistributes shares but never enlarges the pool. Aon's 2027 data confirms the sector gap (India avg 9.1%, IT services 6.6% and the lowest sector, tech products 9.5%, NBFCs 10.1%), so a top rating in a 6.6% sector is dividing a structurally smaller cake than a product firm's.

sources.quote: Technology Consulting and Services at 6.6% represents the minimum growth rate across all industries in the survey; Technology Platform and Products are projected at 9.5% and NBFCs at 10.1%, against an overall India projection of 9.1%.

Before the matrix is applied, the merit budget is set and modeled, eligibility is confirmed, and performance ratings are calibrated — Finance weighs revenue forecasts, inflation and labor-market movement to size the pool, which Compensation then translates into guidelines benchmarked against external survey sources.
